name: The Event Horizon
kick: gravity & light · first principles · where inward becomes the only future
title: The event horizon — a one-way causal boundary, not a wall
lede: A black hole doesn't 'suck you in' like a drain. Instead, its gravity warps space and time so severely that past a certain boundary — the event horizon — the geometry of the future leaves no path that goes outward. It's not that something holds you in; it's that 'outward' ceases to exist. Here is how a boundary defined purely by cause-and-effect reshapes what we know about gravity, time, and the universe itself.
arc: Why it's a horizon, not a wall

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — what actually holds you in?

blocks.html: A black hole's pull is so strong that even light cannot escape. But think about that carefully. Gravity pulls on things by warping the space around them — curves space a little, and objects veer slightly from a straight line. Pull on the curvature harder, and the veer grows. Yet a 'pull' is still just a direction, a push toward lower altitude. So at the event horizon, where light itself — the fastest thing in the universe — must turn around and fall inward, what exactly is the mechanism? What holds the light in? Why can't it simply turn and flee outward?

The puzzle sharpens when you ask: what does an astronaut feel at the horizon? If nothing holds, if it is just space curving, then locally — right where the astronaut is — shouldn't space look ordinary? Yet somehow crossing that line erases 'escape' from possibility. The stakes are clear: an event horizon is not a physical wall or a trap that grabs you — it is a boundary in cause-and-effect itself.

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — inside a horizon, all futures point inward

blocks.html: Einstein's geometry shows that near a compact mass, the shape of spacetime — the way space and time are knitted together — warps. Move closer to the mass, and that warping grows. At some special radius called the Schwarzschild radius, the warping becomes extreme: the future-cone of possibilities — every path a light beam or any object can follow going forward in time — tips inward. To put it plainly: if you are inside the event horizon and you send out a light signal (the fastest possible messenger), that light still must go forward in time, and the warped geometry forces it inward. There is no outward-pointing future. The horizon is the last place where 'outward at light speed' is still possible.

A critical clarity: a freely falling astronaut feels nothing special at the moment of crossing. Locally, spacetime looks flat — ordinary. It is only from the outside that the horizon appears as a boundary of no return, because the geometry ahead has tilted all futures inward. The boundary is defined not by force or structure, but by the topology of cause-and-effect: which points in the universe can send a signal to which other points.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — computing the event horizon for real masses

blocks.html: We computed the Schwarzschild radius — the radius to which a mass must be compressed for its event horizon to form — from the mass and the speed of light. These are measured facts about our universe, not theory.

blocks.caption: To trap light, the Sun would have to be squeezed into a sphere 2.95 km across (about the width of a small town). Earth would fit inside a marble.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: for the Sun's mass that boundary sits at 2.95 km radius; for Earth's mass at about 8.9 mm. Cross that threshold and no light — no signal of any kind — can ever reach the outside world. A collapsing star the size of our Sun would form an event horizon as wide as a small city; a mass the size of Earth would form one inside a marble. These radii are not arbitrary — they follow from the exact ratio of the mass to the speed of light (and Newton's gravitational constant). Every mass has its horizon radius, even yours; yours is fantastically tiny because your mass is small.

sections.h2: 4 · Why it's a horizon, not a wall — the geometry of forward-time

blocks.html: Imagine standing just outside the horizon, looking inward. The 'wall' you picture is nowhere to be found — the spacetime there is smooth, no barrier. Yet a light signal aimed outward cannot escape. Why? Because time and space are woven together by the geometry. Deep inside a horizon, the direction 'outward in space' and the direction 'forward in time' have swapped roles in a profound way. Moving outward is like moving backward in time — and nothing can move backward in time. So there is no escape not because a wall blocks it, but because the shape of spacetime makes outward incompatible with going forward.

This is why an astronaut crossing the horizon feels nothing in the moment: locally, spacetime is nearly flat, ordinary. But their future is sealed not by force, but by the large-scale geometry. Every possible path forward in time takes them deeper inward. The horizon is a coordinate surface — a one-way membrane in cause-and-effect, not a physical thing.

sections.h2: 5 · The one real limit — this picture breaks near spin and at scales where quantum reigns

blocks.html: The clean Schwarzschild-radius picture assumes a nonrotating black hole, perfectly spherical and eternal. Real black holes spin, and spinning black holes have two horizons (an outer causal boundary and an inner one), with a strange region between. Spinning also opens a mathematical loophole — paths that look closed to the outside world — that the full analysis must handle. And the whole classical picture (even the tidy causal picture) breaks down near the horizon's scale, where quantum effects take over. Hawking showed that quantum fluctuations at the horizon cause black holes to emit radiation and evaporate, so no black hole is truly eternal. The 'one-way causal boundary' is a clean classical picture; the real universe is messier.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — causal boundaries reshape physics

blocks.html: The idea of a boundary defined by 'what can send a signal to what' started as a way to understand black holes. It became far larger. Every observer in an expanding universe has a cosmological horizon — a sphere beyond which no light signal from there will ever reach them, not because something blocks it but because space is stretching faster than light can travel. The Earth and the Sun share a common cosmological horizon beyond which we can never send a signal or be reached. By framing horizons as causal surfaces, not physical walls, Einstein's work fused gravity with causality and time — tying black holes to entropy, leading to the information paradox (where does information go if it crosses the horizon?), and hinting at deep relationships between thermodynamics and the geometry of spacetime itself.

A horizon is therefore not a black-hole curiosity; it is a fingerprint of how geometry, causality, and thermodynamics are woven together in a universe ruled by gravity. Trace the shape of a horizon and you read the deep structure of what is possible.

recipe.summary: Compute the Schwarzschild radius (the event horizon radius) from the mass and the speed of light using r_s = 2GM/c². For the Sun (M = 1.989 × 10³⁰ kg) this gives 2.95 km; for Earth (M = 5.972 × 10²⁴ kg) this gives 8.9 mm. numpy, SI units.
recipe.eq:
Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c²
Sun: r_s = 2.95 km
Earth: r_s = 8.9 mm

Inside r_s, every possible future-directed path leads inward (spacetime is so curved that 'outward' is no longer a forward-time direction).
recipe.note: Full script: scripts/experiments/gr_run.py (EXP6). Numbers are the run's output verbatim. The Schwarzschild radius is a coordinate surface defined by g_tt = 0 in the Schwarzschild metric; it is where light can no longer escape.
